gloss: To want something strongly.
examples: Most parents *desire* a better life for their children.
She had long *desired* a place of her own.
He got everything he had ever *desired* and still felt empty.

gloss: To rob a place of its beauty or its valuable things.
examples: Cheap development can *despoil* an entire coastline.
The invaders *despoiled* every village along the river.
The valley has been *despoiled* by decades of strip mining.

gloss: To make a country, a system or a situation less steady and more likely to fail.
examples: A rumor like that can *destabilize* the whole market.
The coup *destabilized* the region for a decade.
The currency has been *destabilized* by months of protest.
contrast: American *destabilize*; British *destabilise*.

gloss: To make people stop treating something as shameful.
examples: The campaign is trying to *destigmatize* asking for help.
That one film *destigmatized* therapy for a lot of viewers.
Mental illness is slowly being *destigmatized* in the workplace.

gloss: To set someone or something aside in advance for a particular purpose or fate.
examples: Nothing in his childhood seemed to *destine* him for politics.
Her parents *destined* her for medicine before she could walk.
The plan was *destined* to fail from the very first meeting.
contrast: Almost always passive: *be destined for* something, *be destined to* do something.

gloss: To separate hair, cords or threads that have become knotted together.
examples: This spray helps *detangle* wet hair.
She *detangled* the headphone cords before packing them.
We spent an hour *detangling* the Christmas lights.

transitivity: both — transitive (*detox* the body), intransitive (he *detoxed* in a clinic)
gloss: To clear alcohol, drugs or other harmful substances out of the body.
examples: He checked into a clinic to *detox*.
She *detoxed* for a week before the surgery.
After three days of *detoxing*, he finally slept through the night.

gloss: To remove poisonous substances from a body, a substance or a place.
examples: The liver *detoxifies* the blood around the clock.
Crews *detoxified* the soil before the park was built.
The patient had to be *detoxified* over two days.
contrast: The y becomes ie before -s and -d: *detoxifies*, *detoxified*, but *detoxifying* keeps the y.

gloss: To make something seem less good or less valuable.
examples: One weak chapter does not *detract* from the book.
The noise *detracted* from an otherwise perfect evening.
Nothing has *detracted* from her reputation as a teacher.
contrast: Almost always with *from*: *detract from* the value, never 'detract the value'.

transitivity: both — transitive (*devalue* the currency), intransitive (the peso *devalued* sharply)
gloss: To reduce the worth of money, work or a person's contribution.
examples: Printing money like that can *devalue* the currency overnight.
The government *devalued* the peso in August.
Teachers say they feel *devalued* by the new rules.

gloss: To move away from an expected course, plan or standard.
examples: Don't *deviate* from the recipe the first time you make it.
The plane *deviated* from its route to avoid the storm.
He has never *deviated* from that position in public.
contrast: Takes *from*: *deviate from* the plan.

transitivity: both — transitive (*devolve* power to the regions), intransitive (the talks *devolved* into shouting)
gloss: To pass power or duties down to a lower level, or to sink into a worse state.
examples: Arguments like that usually *devolve* into name-calling.
The debate quickly *devolved* into a shouting match.
Most of these decisions have been *devolved* to the states.
contrast: *Devolve into* means to deteriorate into; *devolve to* means to be handed down to.

gloss: To stop living.
examples: Plants *die* quickly without water.
His grandfather *died* last spring.
The battery is *dying* and the screen keeps going black.
contrast: The -ing form drops ie for y: *dying*, never 'dieing'. Do not confuse it with *dye — dyed — dyeing*, which means to color cloth.

gloss: To be unlike something else, or to hold a different opinion.
examples: The two reports *differ* on almost every number.
Their accounts *differed* in one crucial detail.
Historians have *differed* about the cause for a century.
contrast: *Differ from* means to be unlike; *differ with* means to disagree with. The stress is on the first syllable, so the r does not double: *differed*, *differing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*diffuse* the light), intransitive (the smell *diffused* through the room)
gloss: To spread something out over a wide area, or to spread out in that way.
examples: Thin curtains *diffuse* the afternoon light nicely.
The smell of coffee *diffused* through the whole apartment.
The heat is *diffused* evenly by the metal plate.
contrast: Not *defuse* (dee-FYOOZ), which means to make a bomb or a tense situation safe. The adjective *diffuse* ends in an s sound: dih-FYOOS.

gloss: To treat something as worthy of serious attention or respect.
examples: I won't *dignify* that question with an answer.
He *dignified* the small ceremony simply by showing up.
The rumors have never been *dignified* with a response.
contrast: The y becomes ie before -s and -d: *dignifies*, *dignified*, but *dignifying* keeps the y.

gloss: To wander away from the main subject while speaking or writing.
examples: But I *digress* — back to the main point.
The lecturer *digressed* for ten minutes about his cat.
He kept *digressing* until we ran out of time.

transitivity: both — transitive (the drops *dilate* the pupils), intransitive (her pupils *dilated*)
gloss: To make an opening in the body wider, or to become wider.
examples: Your pupils *dilate* in the dark.
The doctor *dilated* her eyes before the exam.
He arrived with his pupils still *dilated* from the drops.

gloss: To make something dirty.
examples: Take your shoes off so you don't *dirty* the rug.
The kids *dirtied* every towel in the house.
Her white coat was *dirtied* by spray from the road.
contrast: The y becomes ie before -s and -d: *dirties*, *dirtied*, but *dirtying* keeps the y.

gloss: To free someone of a belief that is not true.
examples: Let me *disabuse* you of that idea right now.
One week on the job *disabused* her of any romantic notions about it.
He has been *disabused* of the belief that hard work is always enough.
contrast: Takes *of*: *disabuse someone of* an idea.

gloss: To stop being visible, or to stop existing.
examples: Socks *disappear* in this building's laundry room.
The sun *disappeared* behind the clouds.
Two hikers have *disappeared* in the park this month.
contrast: Spelling trap: one s but two p's — *disappear*, *disappeared*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the board *disapproved* the request), intransitive (my parents *disapprove* of him)
gloss: To think that something is bad or wrong.
examples: My parents *disapprove* of the whole plan.
The committee *disapproved* the request without a hearing.
She has always *disapproved* of gossip.
contrast: In the everyday sense it takes *of*: *disapprove of* smoking.

gloss: To take a machine or a structure apart into its separate pieces.
examples: You have to *disassemble* the bed to get it through the door.
He *disassembled* the engine on the kitchen table.
The stage was *disassembled* in under an hour.
contrast: Not *dissemble*, which means to hide your real feelings.

gloss: To say publicly that you have no connection with something or no longer support it.
examples: The senator was quick to *disavow* the ad.
The group *disavowed* any link to the attack.
He has publicly *disavowed* everything he wrote back then.

ru: лишать адвокатского статуса, лишить права практики
gloss: To take away a lawyer's right to practice law.
examples: The state can *disbar* an attorney for stealing from clients.
The court *disbarred* him two years ago.
She was *disbarred* after the fraud came to light.
contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable, so the r doubles: *disbarred*, *disbarring*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the jury *disbelieved* him), intransitive (she had no reason to *disbelieve*)
gloss: To refuse to accept that something is true.
examples: I have no reason to *disbelieve* her.
The jury clearly *disbelieved* the witness.
His account was *disbelieved* by everyone in the room.

gloss: To pay out money from a fund that has been set aside.
examples: The foundation will *disburse* the grants in May.
The agency *disbursed* four million dollars last year.
Aid has already been *disbursed* to three provinces.
contrast: Not *disperse* (to scatter). *Disburse* is about paying money out.

gloss: To state officially that you have no responsibility for something or no claim to it.
examples: The site *disclaims* any responsibility for what users post.
The company *disclaimed* all knowledge of the leak.
He has *disclaimed* his share of the inheritance in writing.

transitivity: both — transitive (coffee *discolors* teeth), intransitive (the pages *discolored* with age)
gloss: To change the color of something for the worse, usually by staining or fading.
examples: Coffee will *discolor* your teeth over time.
The sun *discolored* the curtains in a single summer.
The wall was *discolored* where the water got in.
contrast: American *discolor, discolored*; British *discolour, discoloured*.

gloss: To make someone feel uneasy or unsure of themselves.
examples: A silence like that can *disconcert* even a good speaker.
His steady stare *disconcerted* her.
The audience was *disconcerted* by the sudden blackout.

gloss: To make people stop believing or respecting someone or something.
examples: The defense tried to *discredit* the witness.
New data *discredited* the original study.
The theory has been thoroughly *discredited*.

transitivity: both — transitive (they *disembarked* the passengers first), intransitive (we *disembarked* at noon)
gloss: To get off a ship, a plane or a train.
examples: Passengers *disembark* through the rear door.
We *disembarked* in Naples at dawn.
The troops had already *disembarked* by midnight.

gloss: To make someone stop believing that something is as good as they thought.
examples: A year in the industry can *disenchant* almost anyone.
The scandal *disenchanted* many longtime fans.
Voters have grown *disenchanted* with both parties.
contrast: Usually passive, with *with*: *disenchanted with* politics.

gloss: To free something from knots, or to separate things that have become confused with each other.
examples: It took an hour to *disentangle* the fishing line.
She *disentangled* herself from the argument and left.
The two firms are still *disentangling* their finances.

gloss: To spoil the appearance of a person or a thing badly.
examples: Graffiti *disfigures* half the buildings on the block.
The fire *disfigured* his hands.
The statue was badly *disfigured* by vandals.

gloss: To make someone lose hope or confidence.
examples: Three rejections in a row would *dishearten* anyone.
The result *disheartened* the whole team.
She was *disheartened* by how little had changed.

gloss: To bring shame on someone, or to refuse to honor an agreement or a check.
examples: Breaking that promise would *dishonor* everyone who fought for it.
The bank *dishonored* the check.
He felt *dishonored* by the accusation.
contrast: American *dishonor*; British *dishonour*. The h is silent: dis-AH-nur.

gloss: To show someone that what they believed in is not as good or true as they thought.
examples: I hate to *disillusion* you, but the job isn't glamorous.
Two years in politics *disillusioned* him completely.
Many young doctors are *disillusioned* with the system.

gloss: To arrange legally that someone will not receive your property after your death.
examples: He threatened to *disinherit* all three children.
She *disinherited* her nephew in the final will.
The son was *disinherited* without any explanation.

gloss: To force something or someone out of a fixed position.
examples: Use a stick to *dislodge* the ball from the gutter.
The storm *dislodged* several roof tiles.
The champion has not been *dislodged* in six years.

gloss: To cut a body apart, or to break a country or an organization into pieces.
examples: The plan would *dismember* the company and sell the pieces.
The treaty *dismembered* the old empire.
The estate was *dismembered* and sold off in lots.

ru: спешиваться, слезать (с лошади, велосипеда); снимать с крепления
transitivity: both — transitive (*dismount* the camera), intransitive (riders must *dismount*)
gloss: To get down from a horse or a bicycle, or to take something off its mounting.
examples: Riders must *dismount* before crossing the bridge.
She *dismounted* and led the horse to the barn.
The lens had already been *dismounted* and packed away.

gloss: To make someone lose their sense of where they are or what is happening.
examples: Bright lights and loud music can *disorient* you fast.
The fog *disoriented* even the local guides.
She woke up cold and completely *disoriented*.
contrast: American English prefers *disorient*; British English usually says *disorientate*.

gloss: To speak about someone or something as though they have little value.
examples: I don't want to *disparage* anyone's work here.
He *disparaged* his opponent at every stop on the tour.
Her research was *disparaged* for years before it was accepted.

gloss: To make a feeling or a false belief go away.
examples: Let me *dispel* a few myths about the test.
Her calm voice *dispelled* the panic in the room.
The rumor was quickly *dispelled* by the photos.
contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable, so the l doubles: *dispelled*, *dispelling*.

gloss: To annoy someone or make them unhappy.
examples: Any decision here is bound to *displease* somebody.
The tone of the letter *displeased* her.
He was clearly *displeased* with the result.

transitivity: both — transitive (the news *disposed* him to accept), intransitive (*dispose* of the packaging)
gloss: To get rid of something, or to make someone inclined to feel or act a certain way.
examples: Please *dispose* of the packaging in the blue bin.
The court *disposed* of the case in a single morning.
She seemed *disposed* to give him another chance.
contrast: In the 'get rid of' sense it always takes *of*: *dispose of the trash*, never 'dispose the trash'.

gloss: To take land, a home or property away from the person who owns it.
examples: The new law let the state *dispossess* absentee owners.
The war *dispossessed* millions of farmers.
Families *dispossessed* in the 1950s are still seeking compensation.

ru: игнорировать, пренебрегать; не принимать во внимание
gloss: To pay no attention to something, especially something you should consider.
examples: Please *disregard* the last email.
He *disregarded* every warning on the label.
The jury was told to *disregard* the remark.

gloss: To insult someone or treat them with open disrespect, in informal speech.
examples: Don't *diss* the food before you've tried it.
He *dissed* her in front of the whole class.
She felt *dissed* by the way they announced it.
contrast: Informal. The s doubles: *dissed*, *dissing*. Also written *dis*.

gloss: To fail to give someone what they wanted or expected.
examples: A wait that long will *dissatisfy* even a loyal customer.
The settlement *dissatisfied* both sides.
Many employees are *dissatisfied* with the new schedule.
contrast: Two s's in the middle, and the y becomes ie before -s and -d: *dissatisfies*, *dissatisfied*.

gloss: To cut something open to study it, or to examine an idea part by part.
examples: We had to *dissect* a frog in biology class.
Analysts *dissected* every line of the speech.
The play has been *dissected* by critics for a century.

gloss: To spread information widely to many people.
examples: The agency will *disseminate* the new guidelines next week.
The group *disseminated* the report to every member.
The findings have been widely *disseminated* online.

gloss: To disagree openly with an official decision or a majority opinion.
examples: Two justices *dissent* in almost every case of this kind.
Only one board member *dissented*.
He has *dissented* from the party line more than once.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *descent* (a way down) and close to *decent* (respectable). Usually *dissent from*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*dissociate* the two questions), intransitive (the molecule *dissociates* in water)
gloss: To separate one thing from another, or to declare that you have no connection with something.
examples: He tried to *dissociate* himself from the campaign.
The board *dissociated* itself from the remarks within an hour.
The two problems cannot easily be *dissociated*.
contrast: Also written *disassociate* with the same meaning, but *dissociate* is the standard form. Takes *from*.

gloss: To persuade someone not to do something.
examples: Nothing I said could *dissuade* her.
His parents *dissuaded* him from dropping out.
He was not *dissuaded* by the price.
contrast: The opposite of *persuade*, and it takes *from* + -ing: *dissuaded him from going*.

gloss: To make it clear that you are not connected with someone or something.
examples: Politicians hurry to *distance* themselves from a scandal.
She *distanced* herself from the group's statement.
The brand has *distanced* itself from the old ads.
contrast: Nearly always reflexive: *distance yourself from* something.
